title: Therapeutic interventions
blurb: Recognise the nine therapeutic approaches in Annexe A and choose the right one for the person in front of you.
question: Mr Doyle, 48, drinks heavily. He tells the nurse, "I know it's doing me harm, but it's the only thing that helps me relax." Which response best reflects a motivational interviewing approach?

teach.body: Annexe A 3 of the NMC proficiencies lists nine therapeutic approaches every registered nurse should recognise and use where appropriate: motivational interviewing, solution-focused therapies, reminiscence, talking therapies, de-escalation, CBT techniques, play, distraction and diversion, and positive behaviour support. In plain English: these are structured ways of talking and acting that help a person change, cope or feel safer. The CBT asks you to match the approach to the person and the situation.
teach.cite: NMC Standards of proficiency (2018) Annexe A 3.1-3.9

teach.h: Motivational interviewing: resolve ambivalence, don't argue
teach.body: NICE describes the key elements of motivational interviewing as helping people recognise problems, helping to resolve ambivalence, encouraging belief in their ability to change, and taking a supportive rather than argumentative or confrontational position. So you ask open questions about the good and less good things about the behaviour and reflect back what you hear. Lecturing about harm usually produces resistance.

teach.caption: NHS: CBT helps you change how you think and act; sessions involve questioning unhelpful thoughts and changing what you do.

steps.label: Distract and negotiate
steps.sub: Offer choices; known triggers in care plan

steps.label: Restrictive step
steps.sub: Last resort if harm likely; keep de-escalating

teach.body: For a person with a learning disability whose behaviour challenges, NICE NG11 asks for a functional assessment: describe the behaviour, identify what predicts it (events, times, situations) and what maintains it (its function). The behaviour support plan then changes the environment (for example reducing noise, increasing predictability), teaches a new way to meet the same need, and uses calming and distraction early.

teach.h: Scenario: Ellie on the children's ward
teach.body: Ellie, 5, needs a cannula tomorrow and is frightened. Today the play specialist uses a doll with a cannula so Ellie can see and touch what will happen (therapeutic play). During the procedure the nurse blows bubbles and Ellie counts them (distraction). Two approaches, two moments: play prepares and helps her express feelings; distraction reduces distress during the procedure itself.

teach.text: Play and distraction are not the same thing. Therapeutic play happens BEFORE (or after) a procedure to explain and let the child express feelings; distraction is used DURING the procedure to shift attention. Equally, solution-focused work looks for exceptions ("when is it better?"), whereas CBT examines the evidence for and against a thought.

items: MI: open questions, reflect, resolve ambivalence; supportive not confrontational (NICE CG115).
Solution-focused: goals, strengths and exceptions. CBT: question unhelpful thoughts and change actions.
Reminiscence: memories, photos, music; NICE NG97 suggests considering group reminiscence in mild to moderate dementia.
De-escalation first; restrictive interventions are a last resort (NICE NG10).
PBS: functional assessment, then change the environment and teach new skills (NICE NG11).

summary: You can now recognise the nine therapeutic approaches named in Annexe A 3 and pick the right one for a scenario. You know what makes motivational interviewing, solution-focused and CBT techniques different, and why de-escalation and functional assessment come first.

A.q: Mr Doyle, 48, says, "I know drinking is harming me, but it's the only thing that helps me relax." Which response best reflects motivational interviewing?
options: "What are the good and the less good things about drinking for you?"
"Drinking at that level is seriously damaging your liver, you know."
"You need to cut down to 14 units a week, spread over three days."
"Have you thought about attending a local support group instead?"
A.why: MI helps resolve ambivalence through open questions and a supportive, non-confrontational stance (NICE CG115 rec 1.3.1.1; Annexe A 3.1).

whyNot.1: Warning about harm is confrontational and tends to provoke resistance.
whyNot.2: Giving a target is advice-giving, not exploring his own reasons for change.
whyNot.3: This jumps to a solution before he has explored his mixed feelings.

A.q: A community nurse asks Kofi, 30, "Think of a recent day when things felt a little better. What was different?" Which approach is the nurse using?
options: Cognitive behavioural therapy technique
Motivational interviewing technique
Solution-focused therapy approach
Reminiscence therapy approach
A.why: Asking about exceptions, times when the problem was less present, builds on existing strengths: a solution-focused technique (Annexe A 3.2).

whyNot.0: CBT techniques examine the evidence for and against unhelpful thoughts.
whyNot.1: MI explores ambivalence about a specific change.
whyNot.3: Reminiscence uses memories, photographs or music to support wellbeing and identity.

A.q: On a ward for older people, a nurse uses old photographs and music from the 1960s to talk with Mrs Price, 86, who has dementia, about her life. What is this?
options: Cognitive behavioural therapy
Reminiscence therapy
Distraction and diversion
Solution-focused therapy
A.why: Reminiscence uses memories, photographs and music to support wellbeing and identity (Annexe A 3.3); NICE NG97 rec 1.4.3 suggests considering group reminiscence in mild to moderate dementia.

whyNot.0: CBT works on the link between thoughts, feelings and actions.
whyNot.2: Distraction shifts attention away during a distressing moment, rather than exploring life history.
whyNot.3: Solution-focused therapy works towards goals using strengths and exceptions.

B.q: Tara, 22, says, "I always fail at everything." The nurse asks her to list examples that support and contradict this thought. Which approach is this?
options: A solution-focused technique
A motivational interviewing technique
A reminiscence technique
A cognitive behavioural technique
B.why: Weighing evidence for and against an unhelpful thought is a CBT technique (Annexe A 3.6); the NHS describes CBT as questioning unhelpful thoughts and considering other ways of looking at things.

whyNot.0: Solution-focused work looks for times things went better, not evidence about a belief.
whyNot.1: MI explores ambivalence about change, not the accuracy of a thought.
whyNot.2: Reminiscence draws on past memories to support identity and wellbeing.

B.q: Omar, 7, is anxious while a blood sample is being taken. Which intervention is most appropriate during the procedure itself?
options: Distract him with bubbles, a game or a story
Show him on a doll what the needle will do
Explain each step of the procedure in detail
Ask his parent to wait outside until it is over
B.why: Distraction and diversion reduce procedural distress during the procedure (Annexe A 3.8).

whyNot.1: Doll play is preparation, best done before the procedure (Annexe A 3.7).
whyNot.2: Detailed explanation during the procedure can increase anxiety in a young child.
whyNot.3: A parent's presence usually comforts a child; sending them out removes support.

B.q: On an acute ward, Mr Stone, 40, is pacing and shouting that he wants to leave. He has not harmed anyone. What is the nurse's most appropriate first action?
options: Ask security to stand by the ward exit doors
Speak calmly, keep a safe distance and listen
Offer him p.r.n. medication to help him settle
Tell him firmly that he must return to his bed
B.why: De-escalation comes first: communicate respect and empathy, respect personal space and avoid provocation (NICE NG10 recs 1.3.12-1.3.17; Annexe A 3.5; Code 13.4 own safety).

whyNot.0: A show of security may provoke him before de-escalation has been tried.
whyNot.2: Medication is considered after verbal de-escalation, not as the first step.
whyNot.3: Firm instructions at a flashpoint risk provoking aggression.

C.q: Sam, 26, has a learning disability and hits out in the noisy dining room at mealtimes. The team wants to use positive behaviour support. What should happen first?
options: Arrange for him to eat by himself in his room at every meal
Agree a restraint plan with the team for mealtimes
Assess what triggers the behaviour and what it achieves
Ask his GP to review him for a sedative before meals
C.why: NICE NG11 rec 1.5.9: a functional assessment identifies what predicts the behaviour and what maintains it, which then shapes a behaviour support plan (Annexe A 3.9).

whyNot.0: Isolating him without understanding the behaviour is restrictive and may not meet his needs.
whyNot.1: Restrictive responses are reactive strategies, not the starting point of PBS.
whyNot.3: NICE does not support medication as a first response before the behaviour is understood.

C.q: Jodie, 35, has low mood. She asks the nurse whether she needs to see her GP to get talking therapy for anxiety and depression. What is the most accurate answer?
options: She needs a GP referral before any NHS service will see her
She can refer herself to NHS Talking Therapies in most areas
She must first be assessed by a community mental health team
She can access it after a formal diagnosis from a psychiatrist
C.why: The NHS website states adults (18+, or 16+ in some areas) can refer themselves to NHS Talking Therapies for anxiety and depression without seeing a GP (Annexe A 3.4).

whyNot.0: A GP referral is needed for some conditions such as eating disorders or psychosis, not for anxiety and depression.
whyNot.2: A CMHT assessment is not required to access NHS Talking Therapies.
whyNot.3: The NHS states you do not need a diagnosed mental health condition to get CBT.

C.q: Ms Ward, 52, smokes and says she wants to stop "but not yet". The nurse wants to use motivational interviewing. Which response best fits?
options: "Most people find it easier with medication, so let's book you in."
"If you don't stop now, your risk of lung disease will keep rising."
"Let's set a quit date for next Monday and plan around that."
"What would need to change for you to feel ready to stop?"
C.why: An open, evocative question explores her ambivalence and belief in her ability to change, the key elements of MI (NICE CG115 rec 1.3.1.1; Annexe A 3.1).

whyNot.0: Booking treatment before she is ready bypasses her ambivalence.
whyNot.1: Warnings are confrontational and tend to increase resistance.
whyNot.2: Imposing a quit date is directive, not exploring her own motivation.

reteach.title: Match the tool to the moment
reteach.question: If each approach is a different tool, which situation calls for which one?

blocks.h: Ask: what is happening right now?
blocks.body: Mixed feelings about change call for motivational interviewing. A person stuck in a problem who has had better days suits solution-focused questions. Unhelpful thoughts suit CBT techniques. Rising anger needs de-escalation now. A child facing a procedure needs play before and distraction during. Repeated behaviour that challenges in a person with a learning disability needs positive behaviour support, which starts with understanding the behaviour's function.

blocks.h: A child's procedure: which approach when

blocks.text: "When is it better?" is solution-focused. "What's the evidence for that thought?" is CBT. "What are the good and less good things?" is MI.

explain.body: Helps people recognise problems, resolve ambivalence and believe they can change, from a supportive, not confrontational, position (NICE CG115). Use open questions and reflect back what you hear.

test.q: Which statement by a nurse is most consistent with motivational interviewing?
options: "You really must stop before it causes a stroke."
"I'd recommend nicotine patches as a first step."
"It sounds like part of you wants to stop."
"Your blood pressure shows you need to stop."
test.why: Reflecting the person's own wish for change is a core MI skill that helps resolve ambivalence.

whyNot.1: This is advice-giving before exploring motivation.
whyNot.3: Using results to tell the person what to do is directive, not evocative.

explain.body: Solution-focused work asks about goals and exceptions ("when is it a little better?") and builds on strengths. CBT techniques link thoughts, feelings and actions: questioning unhelpful thoughts and changing what you do, often with practice between sessions.

test.q: A nurse helps Mr Reid notice that he avoids the shops because he thinks people stare, and plans a short trip to test this. Which approach is this?
options: Solution-focused therapy
Reminiscence therapy
Positive behaviour support
A CBT technique
test.why: Testing an unhelpful thought by changing behaviour (doing something avoided) is a CBT technique.

whyNot.0: Solution-focused work looks for exceptions and goals rather than testing a belief.
whyNot.2: PBS is used for behaviour that challenges, often in people with a learning disability.

explain.body: Recognise early signs, separate the person from others to a quieter space without isolating staff, communicate respect and empathy, respect personal space and avoid provocation. Restrictive interventions are a last resort, and de-escalation continues throughout (NICE NG10).

test.q: Which action best supports de-escalation with an agitated patient?
options: Standing close to show you are in control
Moving the patient to a quieter space with staff
Telling the patient their behaviour is unacceptable
Asking other patients to watch from a distance
test.why: NICE NG10 rec 1.3.14: separate agitated people from others using quieter spaces, ensuring staff do not become isolated.

whyNot.0: Invading personal space can provoke aggression.
whyNot.2: Confronting behaviour at a flashpoint tends to escalate it.
whyNot.3: An audience increases pressure and risk.

explain.body: A functional assessment describes the behaviour, what predicts it and what maintains it. The plan then makes proactive changes (less noise, more predictability), teaches a new skill to meet the same need, and uses relaxation and distraction early (NICE NG11).

test.q: What is the purpose of a functional assessment in positive behaviour support?
options: To decide which restraint technique is safest
To find out what the behaviour achieves for the person
To measure the person's IQ and overall level of disability
To show the person the consequences of the behaviour
test.why: NICE NG11 rec 1.5.9: identify the reinforcers that maintain the behaviour, that is, the function or purpose it serves.

whyNot.0: Restraint is a reactive strategy, not the aim of functional assessment.
whyNot.2: Functional assessment is about the behaviour, not intelligence testing.
whyNot.3: PBS is proactive and supportive, not consequence-based.
